s1a: You have seen this video. A grandmother talks to a machine. It is patient and funny, she laughs, and it is lovely.
s1c: And it is Tuesday afternoon, and she is still on her own.
s2a: In Italy, two point seven million people over seventy-five live on their own. One household in ten.
s2b: Ninety-three per cent of them can count on a relative. Three in a hundred have nobody at all.
s2c: So this is not abandonment. The families exist. They are at work, or three hours away.
s2d: What is missing is not love. It is the ordinary daily contact, where somebody would simply have noticed.
s2e: Did they take the tablets. Are they eating. He told me the same story twice the last day. There is one person with a key to the house, and he trusts everybody.
s2f: None of it is an emergency. Which is exactly why nobody catches it.
s3a: So, we need a companion: Closer. Not a generic chatbot. Something with a job.
s3b: Every old person was once very good at something. Then the world moved on without them, and stopped asking.
s3c: Peggy ran the sample room at a clothing factory for forty-one years. She can still tell whether a jacket was put together properly, and she is full of memories about it. Nobody has asked her in ten years.
s3d: So the companion asks. And then it tells her what became of her trade after she left.
s4a: This is the actual thing, running.
s4c: It catches a joke and plays along, instead of explaining it.
s5a: It keeps her diary. She says she took her tablets, it writes it down and reads it back, so she can catch a mistake.

s9a: None of this is general. The companion starts knowing the user. The user or somebody close sets it up for one person, in twenty minutes.
s9b: Her week is typed, never guessed. Her circle is hers: habits, relatives, emergencies, or the whole summary.
s9c: And one can add a list it will never raise. The dog that died. Money. Somebody who is gone.
s6a: Her family get a page. It opens with one sentence, and usually that sentence is that nothing happened.
s6b: When something is noticed, it is reported quietly. The page gives one gentle suggestion, and it stays there until one of the allowed relatives has marked it read.
s6c: Five things, at three scales, because a missed walk means one thing in a day and another in a month. Where it has something to say, it says it in her own words.
s7b: It is not a medical device and does not audition for the part. It notices that someone who used to have a walk has not in the last couple of days.
s7b2: That sad words keep recurring. That someone was confused about a daughter's name, or is skipping routines. And tells the people who love her.
s7c: It is built for a person, not a condition. There is no dementia mode. There is a list of voices to choose from, and a name the user gives the companion.
s7d: It also refuses to be told or track a PIN, a personal detail, or financial data. Itself included.
s8a: Every companion app promises the same things. Configurable. Remembers routines. So does this one. That is the entry fee, not the product.
s8b: The difference is what it does with a silence. Other companions wait to be asked. This one arrives with something to say. And if the conversation sounds unusual, alerts the family.
